Brief: Tell me about Alan Turing and elaborate on the impact of his work. — about Death

1. A post mortem was held that evening, which determined that he had died the previous day at age 41 with cyanide poisoning cited as the cause of death.
2. When his body was discovered, an apple lay half-eaten beside his bed, and although the apple was not tested for cyanide, it was speculated that this was the means by which Turing had consumed a fatal dose.
3. Turing's brother, John, identified the body the following day and took the advice given by Franz Greenbaum to accept the verdict of the inquest, as there was little prospect of establishing that the death was accidental.
4. The inquest was held the following day, which determined the cause of death to be suicide.
5. Turing's remains were cremated at Woking Crematorium just two days later on 12 June 1954, with just his mother, brother, and Lyn Newman attending, and his ashes were scattered in the gardens of the crematorium, just as his father's had been.
6. Turing's mother was on holiday in Italy at the time of his death and returned home after the inquest.
7. She never accepted the verdict of suicide.
8. Hodges and a later biographer, David Leavitt, have both speculated that Turing was re-enacting a scene from the Walt Disney film Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937), his favourite fairy tale.
9. Both men noted that (in Leavitt's words) he took "an especially keen pleasure in the scene where the Wicked Queen immerses her apple in the poisonous brew".
10. It has also been suggested that Turing's belief in fortune-telling may have caused his depressed mood.
11. As a youth, Turing had been told by a fortune-teller that he would be a genius.
12. In mid-May 1954, shortly before his death, Turing again decided to consult a fortune-teller during a day-trip to St Annes-on-Sea with the Greenbaum family.
